title: Projectile Motion on an Inclined Plane
learning_objective: Model projectile motion launched onto an inclined plane by orienting coordinate axes parallel and perpendicular to the inclined slope.
intuition: When firing a projectile up a hill of slope angle $\alpha$, gravity no longer pulls straight down relative to the ground you are walking on. By tilting our heads and aligning our coordinate axes so that the $x'$-axis lies along the surface of the hill and the $y'$-axis is perpendicular to it, the problem looks just like a normal projectile problem, except that gravity now has components in both the $x'$ and $y'$ directions.
formal_definition: Let a plane be inclined at angle $\alpha$ to the horizontal. A particle is projected from the base of the plane with speed $u$ at angle $\theta$ with the horizontal (so the launch angle relative to the incline is $\beta = \theta - \alpha$). Choosing the $x'$-axis along the incline upward and $y'$-axis perpendicular upward, the acceleration components are $a_{x'} = -g\sin\alpha$ and $a_{y'} = -g\cos\alpha$. Flight time is determined by $y'(T) = 0 \implies T = \frac{2 u\sin(\theta - \alpha)}{g\cos\alpha}$.
explanation:
Projectile motion on an inclined plane introduces simultaneous acceleration along both coordinate axes.

### 1. Tilted Coordinate System
- Initial velocity components:
  $$u_{x'} = u\cos(\theta - \alpha)$$
  $$u_{y'} = u\sin(\theta - \alpha)$$
- Acceleration components:
  $$a_{x'} = -g\sin\alpha$$
  $$a_{y'} = -g\cos\alpha$$

### 2. Time of Flight and Range
The projectile lands back on the incline when the perpendicular displacement vanishes: $y'(T) = 0$.
$$u_{y'} T - \frac{1}{2} g\cos\alpha T^2 = 0 \implies T = \frac{2 u\sin(\theta - \alpha)}{g\cos\alpha}$$
The range along the incline $R_{\text{up}}$ is given by substituting $T$ into $x'(t)$:
$$R_{\text{up}} = u_{x'} T - \frac{1}{2} g\sin\alpha T^2 = \frac{2 u^2 \sin(\theta - \alpha)\cos\theta}{g\cos^2\alpha}$$

### 3. Condition for Maximum Range
Using trigonometric identity $2\sin(\theta - \alpha)\cos\theta = \sin(2\theta - \alpha) - \sin\alpha$, the range is maximized when $\sin(2\theta - \alpha) = 1$, which yields:
$$2\theta - \alpha = \frac{\pi}{2} \implies \theta_{\text{opt}} = \frac{\pi}{4} + \frac{\alpha}{2}$$
The resulting maximum range up the incline is $R_{\text{max, up}} = \frac{u^2}{g(1 + \sin\alpha)}$.
assumptions: Incline is planar with constant inclination angle $\alpha$.
No bounce or impact dynamics modeled (terminates on contact).
boundary_conditions: Reduces to standard flat ground projectile when $\alpha = 0$, giving $\theta_{\text{opt}} = 45^\circ$ and $R_{\text{max}} = u^2/g$.
Valid strictly for $\theta > \alpha$ (projectile launched above the incline surface).
source_references: Concepts of Physics Vol 1 by H.C. Verma (Chapter 3, pp. 58-60)
